name: Femi Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Femi, thanks for sitting down with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. So you can say what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a council housing refurb on the Eastfield estate, forty flats getting new kitchens, doors and windows while the tenants still live there. I'm a site joiner, second fix mostly: hanging doors, skirting, architrave, fitting kitchen units. I'm in by half seven, and the first job is usually knocking on a door and saying sorry to a pensioner in her dressing gown. Then I measure, cut, fit, clean up, and move on to the next flat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when Mrs Okafor in number twelve makes tea in her new kitchen and tells me it's the first time in twenty years the cupboard doors shut properly. Hardest is the money, honestly. The firm pays below the going rate because there's not much else round here, and with Lena on a teaching assistant's wage we're always about two weeks from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter, like wages and housing. I post a bit in the tenants' and workers' group on my phone, so I'd probably share something there. Mostly I'd say it in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I use one of those AI chat things maybe twice a month, to check a building rule or write a polite message to the site manager when I'm angry. If that's all it ever does, my life doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on like normal. I'd keep my union card, keep doing the odd weekend job fitting a door for a neighbour, and keep trying to get Lena's hours up at the school. Nothing about AI would make me do anything different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if I'm honest, because there's enough to worry about without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'write a polite message when I'm angry'. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the materials were late three days running and we got blamed for being behind. I typed out what I really wanted to say, and asked the AI to make it sound professional. It took out every swear word and somehow I still got my point across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, does anything still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same thing that bothers me now: we fix these flats up, and in ten years they'll sell half of them off. AI didn't do that, people did. That's where I'd put my energy.

S0.say: He'd say it's good news and time to talk about what matters, like wages and housing. He'd share something in the tenants' and workers' group on his phone, but mostly say it in the van.
S0.think: It changes nothing for him: he uses an AI chat tool about twice a month to check a rule or soften an angry message. If that's all it ever does, his life stays the same.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal, keeps his union membership and the odd weekend door-fitting job for neighbours. Keeps trying to get his partner Lena more hours at the school.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved, since there's plenty to worry about already.
S0.quote: I typed out what I really wanted to say, and asked the AI to make it sound professional.
S0.fieldNote: Femi already uses AI lightly and practically, with some humour. His politics are about housing and wages more than technology. He draws a clear line: 'AI didn't do that, people did.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change can be good if workers get a say in it. If a machine can do the heavy lifting, fine, but the savings should go into wages and training, not shareholders. I'd want the union pushing for that in every contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the kitchen side of my job is the bit that'd go first. Flat-pack units are already half built in a factory, and if they come fully fitted on a pallet, that's a third of my week. The doors and the awkward old flats, they'll need people longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it actually happening on a site near us, not before, I'd do a short course on whatever new kit the firm brings in. I'd ask the union rep, Dev, to push for that training on paid time. I'd also start using the AI more for quoting my weekend jobs, so I could pick up more of them for the extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There'd be a little knot in my stomach every time the site manager says 'new process'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you saw it happen nearby. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen three 'revolutions' on site already and two of them were gone in a year. Remember those laser levels that cost a fortune and nobody trusted? I'll move, but I want to see someone else's crew do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ada and Sam about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada's fourteen and thinks I'm a dinosaur. I'd tell her the people who get to choose how the machines are used are the ones who'll do well, so learn to be one of those. Sam's ten, he'd just want to know if the robot can play football.

S1.say: Change can be good if workers have a say and the savings go into wages and training, not to shareholders. He'd want the union pushing for that in every contract.
S1.think: He privately expects the kitchen-fitting part of his week to go first, as units arrive fully built. Doors and awkward old flats will need people for longer.
S1.do: Waits until he sees it on a nearby site, then takes a short course on the firm's new kit, asking union rep Dev to secure paid training time. Uses AI more to quote weekend jobs and pick up extra income.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in his stomach whenever the manager mentions a 'new process'.
S1.quote: I've seen three 'revolutions' on site already and two of them were gone in a year.
S1.fieldNote: Femi is the classic 'show me first' adopter: he will move, but only after someone else's crew proves it. He already knows which third of his week is most at risk. Weekend work is his natural safety valve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this can't be left to the market. The government has to step in straight away: income for people who lose work, a freeze on repossessions, and the companies who gain should pay for it. I'd say that in the group chat, at the union, at the school gates, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is nothing. My job isn't the first to go, robots still struggle with a crooked 1960s doorframe, but the firm would stop hiring and the work would dry up. With barely a month's money saved, it wouldn't take long before we're behind on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The week I believed it, we'd cut the extras: phone contracts down to the cheapest, no holiday, the car kept but only for work. I'd go to the union and say we need a plan now, not in a year. I'd talk to Lena about her picking up more hours, and I'd be honest with the bank early rather than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. I'd be lying awake running numbers, and Lena would catch me doing sums on the back of an envelope at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd use those two years for, before it fully arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze every bit of overtime and weekend work I can, while there's still work. And put a bit by, even if it's a few hundred. Honestly, two years doesn't give a man like me time to become something else, it gives me time to brace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots struggle with a crooked doorframe. Is that a comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about six months, maybe. I joke at work that the robot will take one look at the Eastfield flats and quit. But in this picture the robot doesn't quit, it learns, and then I'm just an expensive man with a chisel.

S2.say: This can't be left to the market: the government must act immediately with income for people who lose work and a freeze on repossessions, paid for by the companies that gain. He'd say it in the group chat, at the union and at the school gates.
S2.think: Two years is nothing; even if robots struggle at first with crooked old doorframes, the firm would stop hiring and work would dry up. With barely a month's savings, mortgage arrears would come fast.
S2.do: Cuts phone contracts, holidays and car use to the bone, and pushes the union for an immediate plan. Talks to Lena about more hours, contacts the bank early, and grabs all overtime and weekend work while it lasts.
S2.feel: Frightened and sleepless, doing sums on envelopes at two in the morning.
S2.quote: In this picture the robot doesn't quit, it learns, and then I'm just an expensive man with a chisel.
S2.fieldNote: He uses humour to cope, then undercuts it himself. Two years means bracing, not changing careers, for someone with his savings. He looks first to the state and the union, and is ready to be open with the bank early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so start planning now. Every big contractor should have to publish what jobs they're automating and when, and fund retraining. I'd push the union to make that a demand on every council contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes it feel like something I could get ahead of. Old housing will need fixing for a long time, and the people living there will still want a human at the door. I think I could move into repairs and adaptations for older and disabled tenants, the stuff the robots would be slowest at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the council's maintenance team what qualifications they need for adaptations work, grab rails, ramps, accessible kitchens. I'd do the evening course if the union can get it funded, and I'd start putting fifty or sixty a month aside. Once it's clear it's coming, I'd move over to that kind of work before the queue forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like I can see the cliff, but there's a path down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm hanging on. With five, I get to choose which bit of my trade to stand on. That's the difference between being pushed and stepping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Tommy, who's sixty-one and can't read well. He's the best door hanger I've ever met. Five years is too short for him to retire and too long for him to keep up, and nobody would build a course for a man like him.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to plan, so planning should start now: big contractors should publish what they're automating and when, and fund retraining. He'd push the union to demand this on council contracts.
S3.think: Five years feels like something he could get ahead of. Old housing needs repairing and tenants will want a person at the door, so he sees a path into adaptations for older and disabled tenants.
S3.do: Asks the council maintenance team what qualifications adaptations work needs and takes an evening course if the union can fund it. Saves fifty or sixty a month and moves into that work once it's clearly coming.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan, like seeing a cliff with a path down.
S3.quote: That's the difference between being pushed and stepping.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year timeline is where Femi turns from bracing to planning, and his chosen niche fits both his trade and his values. His concern for Tommy, an older colleague with poor reading, shows how he thinks about others on the crew. He still wants public funding and union backing for the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Build a proper public retraining scheme now, and make sure housing work stays in public hands so the jobs that are left go to local people. I'd probably go to a council meeting for the first time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel like I could manage. I'd be fifty-three, Ada would be finished with school and maybe college, and we'd have chipped at the mortgage. It's not that I'm not worried, it's that the worry has time to turn into something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the adaptations qualification in the first couple of years, slowly, without giving up the joinery. I'd also learn the robot kit properly when it's being used on a site, because someone has to set it up and check its work. I'd try to get Lena on board with a small savings plan so we're not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It feels like weather you can see coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently for the children, knowing there's a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop telling Ada she has to go to university to be safe, because nobody knows what's safe. I'd tell her to learn things that need people to trust her. And I'd let Sam take things apart in the shed, because whatever's coming, someone will need to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait until others go first. With ten years, would you still wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes for the first few years, that's just me. But I'd be watching, properly, not pretending. When the first crew near us starts using it, I'd be the second, not the tenth.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if it's used: build a public retraining scheme now and keep housing work in public hands so the remaining jobs go to local people. He might attend a council meeting for the first time.
S4.think: Ten years makes it feel manageable: by fifty-three his elder child would have finished school and they'd have chipped at the mortgage. The worry would have time to turn into something useful.
S4.do: Gets the adaptations qualification slowly over the first couple of years without dropping joinery, and learns the robot kit once it's used on local sites. Starts a small savings plan with Lena.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like watching weather come over the hill.
S4.quote: When the first crew near us starts using it, I'd be the second, not the tenth.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Femi stays true to his steady style but sharpens it: he'd still wait, but watch closely and move early in the queue. His advice to his children shifted away from 'go to university to be safe'. His politics turn local and practical, with a first council meeting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With our savings, the fast version is the one where good people lose their homes before anyone in charge has finished arguing. What would help is a guarantee that nobody gets repossessed while they retrain, and training that's paid, local and in the evenings so you can still work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about the workers, but Mrs Okafor and the others on the estate are the ones who'd have a robot in their kitchen. Somebody should ask them how they'd feel about that.

headlineQuote: With our savings, the fast version is the one where good people lose their homes before anyone in charge has finished arguing.
portrait: Femi Novak is a 43-year-old site joiner refitting kitchens and doors on a council estate, with two children, a mortgage and about two weeks between his family and trouble. He uses AI now and then but waits to see other crews prove new things first. AI Plateau leaves him calm, Steady Disruption makes him take a course once it's proven, and AGI by 2028 has him bracing, cutting costs and leaning on the union and the state. With five or ten years he plans a move into adaptations work for older and disabled tenants. He blames decisions made by people, not machines, and wants public, paid, local training.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with his savings good people would lose their homes before anyone in charge acted.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee against repossession while people retrain, and paid, local evening training so he could keep working.
